title: The Burnt Offering: A Whole Gift to God
summary: The LORD calls to Moses from the Tent of Meeting and begins his instructions on offerings with the burnt offering. A worshiper may bring an unblemished male from the herd or the flock, or, if poorer, a turtledove or young pigeon. He lays his hand on the animal's head so that it is accepted on his behalf to make atonement, and the whole animal is burned on the altar as a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
story: Exodus ended with the glory of the LORD filling the tabernacle so completely that Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:35). Leviticus begins at that exact point: God calls to Moses from inside the tent. The question now is how sinful people can come near a holy God who lives among them. The first answer God gives is an offering that holds nothing back. Before the book deals with specific sins, with impurity, or with the Day of Atonement, it begins with an act of complete devotion, the burnt offering, which was the most common and the oldest of Israel's sacrifices. Chapters 1 to 7 go on to describe the grain, peace, sin, and guilt offerings, and chapters 8 and 9 show the system beginning to work.
historical:
Burnt offerings were ancient long before Sinai in Israel's own story. Noah offered them after the flood (Genesis 8:20), Abraham was told to offer Isaac as one before God provided a ram in his place (Genesis 22:2, 13), and Job offered them for his children (Job 1:5). Sacrifice was practiced throughout the ancient Near East. Ritual texts from Ugarit on the Syrian coast, from the late second millennium BC, name a burnt offering and a peace offering among their rites, and Mesopotamian and Egyptian temples offered food to their gods daily. Leviticus shares this world of practice while giving it a different meaning. On the date and authorship of the book, see the introduction to Leviticus: tradition places these instructions at Sinai, while many scholars assign the written form to priestly circles of a later period.

The instructions assume a settled supply of cattle, sheep, goats, and birds. Pastoral groups moving through the Sinai with flocks is plausible for the wilderness setting, and the same laws continued to guide worship later at the temple in Jerusalem, where burnt offerings were made every morning and evening (Exodus 29:38-42) until the temple's destruction in AD 70.
cultural:
In the burnt offering, the whole animal went up in smoke to God; nothing was eaten by the worshiper or the priest, though the priest kept the hide (7:8). That is what made it distinctive among Israel's sacrifices. The ancient Greek translation called it a whole burnt offering, holokautoma, the word from which English later drew holocaust. The worshiper did much of the work himself: he brought the animal to the tent's entrance, laid his hand on its head, slaughtered it, skinned it, and cut it up. The priests handled what belonged to the altar: the blood, the fire, and the arrangement of the pieces. Worship was not a spectator event.

The graded choice of animals mattered. A bull was costly, a sheep or goat less so, and a pair of birds within reach of the poor. Leviticus makes the same provision for other offerings (5:7; 12:8), and Luke 2:24 records that Mary and Joseph offered birds after Jesus' birth, a detail that shows their poverty. The phrase pleasing aroma to the LORD (verses 9, 13, 17) first appears when Noah offers sacrifice (Genesis 8:21). In the Babylonian flood stories the gods go hungry while the flood cuts off their offerings, and in the Epic of Gilgamesh they crowd around the survivor's sacrifice like flies. In Genesis and Leviticus the aroma signifies God's acceptance, not his hunger (compare Psalm 50:12-13).
literary: The chapter opens with a narrative sentence and then becomes case law, set out in three parallel cases introduced by if: an offering from the herd (verses 3-9), from the flock (verses 10-13), and of birds (verses 14-17). Each case follows the same order of actions, and each ends with the same refrain, “it is a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD” (verses 13 and 17, with slight variation in verse 9). The pattern teaches as much as the content: every legitimate offering, whether a bull or two birds, ends in the same acceptance. The Hebrew name of the book, Vayikra, comes from its first word, and he called. In the traditional Hebrew text the last letter of that word is written smaller than the rest, a scribal feature that later Jewish interpreters read as a sign of Moses' humility.

outline.t: The LORD calls to Moses and introduces the offerings
A burnt offering from the herd
A burnt offering from the flock

doctrines.note: Even this offering, which is mainly an act of devotion, is accepted on the worshiper's behalf “to make atonement for him” (verse 4). Before God, every approach by a sinner requires that something be given in his place. Here that is a life wholly given up.
The book begins with God taking the initiative: he calls, he speaks, and he tells his people how to come near. Sacrifice is not humanity's scheme for managing God but God's gift of a way back to him.

The requirement of an unblemished animal and the shedding of blood take for granted that humans cannot approach God simply as they are. Sin and death stand between them, and the offering acknowledges that before any particular sin has been named.

words.note: Olah, burnt offering, from the verb alah, to go up. It is the offering that ascends to God entirely in smoke. It was offered as a freewill gift, as here, and also every morning and evening and at festivals. The name emphasizes that the whole gift goes to God.

Qorban, offering, from qarav, to come near. An offering is literally something brought near, and bringing it brings the worshiper near. The word appears in Mark 7:11 as Corban, a gift devoted to God, where Jesus criticizes using it as an excuse to neglect one's parents.

Samakh, to lean or lay, here the laying of the hand on the animal's head (verse 4). Its meaning is debated: some see it as marking ownership, so the offering counts as truly the worshiper's gift; others see identification or substitution, the animal standing in the worshiper's place. On the Day of Atonement the high priest lays both hands on the goat and confesses the people's sins over it (16:21).

Tamim, unblemished, whole, or complete. The same word describes Noah (Genesis 6:9) and what God asked of Abraham (Genesis 17:1), where it is translated blameless. The animal had to be without defect, because God is not to be offered what is flawed or leftover (compare Malachi 1:8).

christ: The New Testament reads the burnt offering in light of Christ's self-giving. Paul writes that Christ “gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God” (Ephesians 5:2), using the language of the pleasing aroma. Hebrews quotes Psalm 40 as spoken by Christ: “In burnt offerings and sin offerings You took no delight,” and concludes that “we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:6, 10). Peter describes Christ as a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:19). The story of Abraham and Isaac, where God provided the ram for the burnt offering, is often read as pointing in the same direction, since Abraham had said, “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering” (Genesis 22:8). The burnt offering's call for a whole gift also shapes Christian life: Paul urges believers “to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God” (Romans 12:1).

hard.q: Why would God want animals killed and burned?
hard.a:
To many modern readers animal sacrifice seems cruel or primitive. It helps first to see what the text does not say. God does not need food; Psalm 50:12-13 has God ask, “Do I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” Sacrifice in Leviticus is not feeding a hungry deity or buying his favor, as in some neighboring religions. It is a costly gift from a people already rescued, a way of confessing that life belongs to God, and a means God provides for sinners to come near him.

Interpreters emphasize different aspects. Some stress gift and devotion: the worshiper gives something valuable and gives it wholly. Others stress substitution: the animal's life is given in place of the worshiper's, with death acknowledged as the cost of sin (see 17:11). Others stress communion, which is clearer in the peace offering of chapter 3. The prophets insisted that sacrifice without justice and a humble heart was worthless (Psalm 51:16-17; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6-8), but they did not abolish it. Christians believe the sacrifices were fulfilled and ended in Christ's once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10:1-18). Judaism, since the temple's destruction in AD 70, has continued without animal sacrifice, understanding prayer, study, and acts of kindness as its continuation.

questions: The burnt offering held nothing back for the worshiper. What would it look like for you to give something to God without keeping any of it?
God made a way for the poor to offer birds instead of a bull. What does that tell you about how God views what we are able to bring?
The worshiper laid his own hand on the animal and slaughtered it himself. How might that have changed his sense of what it cost to come near God?
